about: Results of the AI editorial review for articles published with the automated label. Not a person's review.

entries.notes: Verified against the ABC Unified Rules of Boxing page (rules 1-13, last amended 3 Aug 2016: 3-minute rounds, mandatory eight count, no standing eight, no three-knockdown rule, 20-second out-of-ring count, no saving by the bell, fair-blow injury = TKO, intentional-foul DQ and mandatory two-point deduction, accidental-foul no decision before four completed rounds and technical decision after, five-minute low-blow allowance); ABC Boxing Referee Manual rev. 08/2025 (knockdown definition, count stops when the standing boxer leaves the neutral corner, gait test, slip signal, re-fall resumes the count, double knockdown = technical draw, a towel cannot stop a US pro bout, low-blow line is the top of the hip not the navel or waistband, soft/hard warning escalation, punch-at-the-bell procedure); Nevada NAC 467.009 (adopts ABC championship rules; chapter controls on conflict), 467.655, 467.675 (32 boxing fouls incl. 'below the navel' and throwing in the towel), 467.688 (points by severity, deducted in that round; a low-blow claim cannot win, refusal = TKO), 467.740/745/757/760; WBC Championship Rules WC-1 (local commission enforces its own rules) and rule 13 (no bell rescue incl. the last round); WBC R&R 3.27 (approved 8 Dec 2024); WBA Rules E.2 (10 or 12 rounds) and E.12 (three knockdowns = automatic KO). Changed: ABC rules now described as model rules 'many state commissions adopt' (not all); rounds sentence rewritten in original words (was a near-paraphrase of Wikipedia); fouls list said 'below the belt' while Nevada's line is the navel - now 'too low', which the article then explains; hard-warning sentence now attributes the deduction step to the referee manual; FAQ and description say rounds are normally three minutes. App paragraph matches the catalog (boxing simulator returns decisions, draws and scorecards; hand speed, power, defence, footwork, ring control); pool described per content-spec rule 10. Links: app page, /sports/combat-sports/, cornerstone boxing-scoring-explained, three published related articles, category page. Verified against ABC Unified Rules of MMA 8.2026 'Types of Decisions' (tap out, verbal tap out, technical submission; TKO = 'IS NOT intelligently defending' by strikes, laceration, corner stoppage, did not answer the bell, or medical stoppage incl. doctor stoppage and loss of bodily function; KO = 'CANNOT' due to strikes; no contest; unanimous/split/majority; technical decision/draw after 2 of 3 or 3 of 5 rounds; DQ for multiple fouls or flagrant disregard) - word-diffed against 8.2025, these definitions are unchanged; ABC boxing rules 11-12; ABC referee manual (physician may stop a bout in most jurisdictions; towel; lost mouthpiece with no spare = TKO; accidental low blow after five minutes = TKO; self-injury = TKO); Nevada NAC 467.718, 467.728, 467.740 (no count in MMA), 467.748(2), 467.702, 467.770, 467.579 (anti-doping win/draw -> no contest), 467.79615, 467.7968; WBC championship rule 15 (technical draw before round 5); WBA E.19 (technical draw before four rounds; draw if cards level). Worked example (round-3 head clash: no decision / no decision / technical draw; round 7 converges) re-derived. Changed: lede and first FAQ said a TKO is a stoppage 'while the fighter is still conscious or still trying', which is wrong for doctor, corner and did-not-answer-the-bell stoppages - now 'covers most other stoppages'; table said a US boxing corner cannot stop a fight - corrected (it can, through the commission inspector and referee, just not by throwing a towel); four-question list now includes the technical draw some rulebooks give for early accidental fouls; 'differs by a single word' and the MMA no-count causal claim softened; added that Nevada lists only physical and verbal tap-outs and defines a KO as unconsciousness from 'a strike, kick or other legal maneuver', so 'a choke-out is a technical submission' is stated as ABC-specific; stated that the 2025 and 2026 texts define results identically; accidental-foul takeaway made specific. Writer's version claim confirmed: the ABC Unified Rules page lists Unified-Rules-of-MMA-8.2026.pdf under 'Current Documents'; its header reads 'AMENDED WITH RULE CHANGES AUGUST 5, 2026, REQUESTED IMPLEMENTATION DATE OF NOVEMEBER 2027' (sic), after the 23 July 2024 rule changes (requested implementation November 2024) and a 1 July 2025 non-substantive amendment. A word-level diff of 8.2025 vs 8.2026 shows the fouls list unchanged and the 2026 changes procedural (standalone loss-of-bodily-function section, nausea/bucket procedure, five-step foul procedure, renumbering), so the article's characterisation, 'as printed' wording and adoption-timetable caveat do not overstate what applies now. Checked in the PDF: fouls numbered 1-27 skipping 10 (26), back-of-head/spine zone, throat, groin, eyes, small joints, pile-driver arc rule, stomping/axe kick, shorts/gloves, fence, eye-poke procedure, five-minute allowance, no timeout for legal strikes without a cut, stand-up quote, replay, equipment, intentional/accidental-foul outcomes and thresholds, non-combat stoppage rule. Nevada verified and dated: NAC 467.7962 still lists 'Striking downward using the point of the elbow' (foul 10) and treats a weight-bearing hand, palm or fist as grounded - section last amended by R032-18 effective 30 Jan 2019, before the July 2024 ABC changes; 467.009(2),(4); 467.7954 (3 rounds non-title, 5 title); 467.427(7) (4-8 oz gloves). CBS Sports (23 Jul 2024) confirms the vote, the old palm-down wording and the 'de-gamify' quote. Calzaghe - Britannica: retired February 2009, undefeated in 46 bouts, 32 by KO. Laila Ali - Britannica: undefeated in 24 bouts, 1999-2007. Kirk 2024 abstract verified via NCBI E-utilities; the PubMed page shows a cookie wall to automated fetch (curl and WebFetch), so the citation now points to the E-utilities record actually opened. Confirmed: n = 2,229 bouts, BF > 3, whole cohort / each year / 13 divisions, ages 29.8 vs 30.7 and 0.82 years younger, armspan advantage at heavyweight only (198.4 +/- 6.6 vs 196.1 +/- 7.7 cm), A:S disadvantage in women's strawweight only, no variable affected method of victory, 'greatly overstated' conclusion. Finlay 2022 (PLOS One full text): 182 bouts April 1991 - January 2022, BoxRec/Wikipedia data, medians 196 vs 190.5 cm height and 201 vs 198 cm reach, d = 0.35 and 0.23, punch-output d = 0.27-0.73, ~8 points accuracy, 41 bouts without punch data. Corrected an overclaim: the article said the paper had 'no reliability data for the variables' (implying reach) - the paper's caution refers to its punch-output table; reach caveats now say the figures came from BoxRec/Wikipedia listings rather than measurement (body, two FAQs, explanation 4 hedged as 'may be noisy'). 'Only a few centimetres' replaced with the exact 5 cm and 7.5 cm; the heavyweight section now notes the boxing study examined only heavyweight, so 'both studies found their clearest effect there' was not like-for-like. Weight-band figures checked against ABC 8.2026 and NAC 467.476; footwork/inside-fighting and 'pressure fighters are often shorter' against Wikipedia. Every study claim checked against the paper or abstract opened. Pollard 1986 abstract (E-utilities): established for all major pro team sports in England and North America, greatest in soccer, ~64% of points, little change since 1888, smaller in derbies/FA Cup/non-professional, larger in the European Cup, familiarity outweighs crowd and travel. Pollard & Pollard 2005 abstract: 400,000+ games from 1876, highest in early years, decline over two decades in ice hockey, basketball and English football, baseball consistently lowest, unbalanced schedules, 'some evidence that travel and familiarity contribute ... little in support of crowd effects'. Pollard 2002 abstract: 37 teams moving within the same city 1987-2001, significant drop (P = 0.011), crowd size/density not explanatory, ~24%. Wunderlich et al. 2021 (PLOS One full text): 40,000+ matches incl. 1,000+ without spectators, foul/yellow/red gaps disappear, shots and shots on target fall, only a non-significant decrease in home advantage, exact 'do not seem to be the main driving factor' quote. Benz & Lopez 2021 (PMC full text): 17 leagues, bivariate Poisson with team strength, goal-HA estimates lower in 11 and higher in 6 incl. EPL and Serie A, yellow-card HA lower in 15 of 17, clear between-league differences pre-Covid. Sedeaud et al. 2021 (PMC): 28.5->32.5% and 38.0->42.8% away wins, Premiership 55.8->45.8% (+/-12.8), Top 14 64.5->55.1, Pro D2 64.6->55.7, 'vanished' in Premiership and Celtic League, limitation that team level and recent form were not considered. Fioravanti et al. (arXiv abstract): 1,027 matches, 11 tournaments, 10 countries. World Rugby (18 Jun 2026): home weighting removed from 1 July 2026, three rating points since 2003, centralised/out-of-country venues, Fiji's three UK 'home' matches, some 20 neutral-venue internationals before end-2026. Arithmetic (38.4/21.6; SE 0.115, difference ~0.16, 1.3 SE) recomputed. Changed: the soccer-vs-rugby paragraph said 'the soccer studies used models that adjust for team strength' - Wunderlich et al. state they did not control for team strength, so it now names Benz & Lopez only; the confounder paragraph now attributes each paper's own caveat (no true control group; disrupted training); 'Home advantage in goals fell in 11 leagues' -> 'their estimate of ...'; lede and description narrowed from 'every major team sport' to the scope Pollard actually studied (England and North America). App claims match the catalog (league campaign in wins/draws/losses; saved runs; 24-match rugby union season); pools described per rule 10. No calculator link: neither permitted tool fits. Every study claim checked against the text opened. Miller & Sanjurjo: Econometrica abstract page (bias proved; shrinks with sequence length, grows with streak length, substantial at lengths used in empirical work; conclusions reversed) and the arXiv full text (1902.01265): 26 Cornell players (14 men, 12 women), 100 shots each at ~50% distance, changing position after every shot; .49 after three hits vs .45 after three misses, not significant; GVT quotes 'analogous to coin tossing' and 'a powerful and widely shared cognitive illusion' (footnote 8); expected difference -8 points for n = 100, p = .5, so +4 is +12 above an i.i.d. shooter; player-level correction +13 points (p < .01); 'consistently moderate to large' across controlled and semi-controlled studies; 'belief in the hot hand is not a cognitive illusion'; players/coaches may infer a non-existent hot hand, overreact or miss one; in-game drop after makes eliminated with partial controls for defence and shot location; the quoted 'the long-standing conclusions of the canonical study are reversed' matches the arXiv wording. Three-shot table recomputed (2.5/6 = 0.417). Wikipedia Hot hand: 1985 questionnaire of 100 fans, 76ers field goals, free throws, controlled experiment. Darts (arXiv 1803.05673 abstract): almost one year, 167,492 throws, minimal interaction, latent-state models, 'a strong but short-lived serial dependence' (exact). Golf (Clark 2005 abstract via E-utilities): 747 tournaments, 35 randomly chosen 1997 professionals, no evidence of a hot hand. Table tennis (Den Hartigh & Gernigon 2018 abstract): 80 players, 1-7 to 7-7 scenarios, time-out at 7-7 cut positive and restored negative momentum, instructions not significant. Overclaim check: null golf result framed with its limits; darts and controlled-shooting results not generalised to in-game play. Changed: the golf app 'answers the opening question with a yes' implied a game design settles a research question - now 'builds momentum into its model'; the rest of the app paragraph matches the catalog verbatim (momentum, confidence, fatigue and pressure within an event; decisions not swing timing; every tour, event and golfer fictional). Barnett, van der Pols & Dobson 2005 (IJE; Cloudflare blocks curl, opened via WebFetch): the quoted definition 'that can make natural variation in repeated data look like real change' is exact, and 'more noticeable with increasing measurement error and when follow-up measurements are only examined on a sub-sample selected using a baseline value' supports the paraphrase. Ben-Naim, Vazquez & Redner (arXiv full text): 300,000+ regular-season games, FA top division and MLB/NHL/NBA/NFL; Table I values matched row by row (the PDF text is garbled, but the text itself confirms MLB sigma = 0.084, baseball narrowest and NFL widest): seasons 1888-2005 / 1901-2005 / 1917-2004 / 1946-2005 / 1922-2004, average games 39.7 / 155.5 / 70.8 / 79.1 / 14.0, upset frequency .452 / .441 / .414 / .365 / .364, sigma .084 (MLB), .150 (NBA), .210 (NFL); method details (location and margin ignored, ties = half a win, equal-record games disregarded) and 'soccer and baseball are the most competitive' confirmed. The chance/ability split is the article's own, clearly labelled calculation and was recomputed (23% / 14% / 40%; 'nearly three times'), as were both worked examples (.577; .627 = 8.8 of 14). Regression formula for equal-variance bivariate normal data, the sophomore slump, Sports Illustrated cover jinx, Kahneman's flight-instructor account and the upward batting-average example are all in the cited Wikipedia article. Added (coordinator-permitted, one link): a sentence linking /tools/multi-sport/pythagorean-expectation-calculator/, with a new source, MLB.com Glossary 'Pythagorean Winning Percentage', which says the formula 'proved more predictive than basic winning percentage when trying to predict a team's future performance'; the tool description matches the tool's own meta (expected record from runs, points or goals). Preflight's note on naming 'MLB' reviewed: nominative citation of a glossary definition, no affiliation implied. Every study claim checked against the abstract or full text opened. Cobley et al. 2009 (abstract): 38 studies 1984-2007, 253 samples, 14 sports, 16 countries; consistent but small; effect grows linearly with relative-age difference; adolescent (15-18) males at regional/national representative level in highly popular sports most affected. Smith et al. 2018 (abstract): 57 studies, 308 samples, 25 sports; OR 1.25 (adjusted 1.21); larger at 11 and under and 12-14, at higher levels and in physically demanding contexts. Brustio et al. 2026 (PMC full text): 26 studies, 318,663 male and 41,379 female players; males 34.8% vs 16.9%, OR 1.99, youth 2.42 vs senior 1.41, U7-U14 2.09 / U15-U17 2.18 / U18-U20 1.52; females 27.5% vs 23.6%, OR 1.15; Trim-and-Fill adjustment to 1.32; substantial heterogeneity; national vs regional difference descriptive but not significant, with 'selection pressures likely amplify' as the authors' reading; underdog hypothesis and transient advantages discussed as hypotheses - the article frames all of these with the authors' own caution.
